title: The Multilingual Artificial Hivemind:Do All LLMs Think Alike in Every Language?

paper.title: The Multilingual Artificial Hivemind: Do All LLMs Think Alike in Every Language?
paper.abstract: Abstract Text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) often remains limited in diversity compared to that produced by humans. Recent advances demonstrate the presence of inter- and intra-model collapse in open-ended generation of English text, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of LLM, and more importantly, human thought. However, our understanding of whether this homogenization extends to languages beyond English is limited. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Specifically, we aim to understand whether multilingual LLM-generated text is also homogeneous, and whether this homogeneity matches what we observe in humans. Across 23 open-weight models and 13 languages, we find that the artificial hivemind effect is pervasive but uneven in its extent. The intra-model effect holds in three different embedding spaces and under a lexical metric that uses no embedding model, so it is not an artifact of how diversity is measured. The size of the homogenization gap is associated with a model’s competence in a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, robustly across embedding spaces. Thus, we demonstrate a performance–diversity tradeoff in multilingual LLMs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have become central in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). As their adoption increases, closer examination of the nature of the generated text is warranted. Specifically, empirical evaluations have revealed an artificial hivemind-like effect in open-ended generation [ 19 ] , defined by high levels of inter- and intra-model homogeneity, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of text on the internet. However, the causes of the observed mode collapse remain unclear. Potential explanations for this phenomenon range from inductive biases inherent to the optimization algorithms used, to the diversity and scale of the training distribution. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Figure 1 : Per-language Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projections of response embeddings. For four representative languages (English, Japanese, Basque, and Chinese), blue point clouds represent the spatial distribution of pooled LLM generations, while red × \times markers display the human answers to the same prompts. LLM generations concentrate into dense modes, whereas the human answers are spread thinly over the same region. Each panel pools all 30 prompts of its language, so it shows the mode structure of the pooled distribution rather than the within-prompt gap measured in Section 4 . Each of the two plotted components explains 5–10% of the embedding variance in its panel. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We evaluate output diversity for 23 LLMs for 13 different languages. • We show that the artificial hivemind effect is, in general, pervasive across languages. • We show the intra-model effect is robust to how diversity is measured, replicating it in three embedding spaces and under an embedder-free lexical metric, and that both effects survive paired prompt-level tests with multiple-comparison correction. • We show that the homogenization gap tracks how well a model handles a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, far more than properties of the language itself such as tokenization cost or morphology.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Our work broadly relates to (i) language model evaluation, and (ii) the development of multilingual LLMs.

sections.heading: 2.1 Language Model Evaluation
sections.text: As language model architectures and capabilities have evolved, so have the evaluations we use to measure progress. Early evaluations of LLMs focused primarily on natural language processing and understanding tasks like question answering and text-summarization [ 21 , 35 , 34 , 29 ] , often relying on metrics like accuracy for single-answer tasks, and the BLEU or F1 score [ 26 ] for open-ended tasks. As LLMs became more capable of reasoning-based tasks [ 14 ] like solving math problems [ 5 , 15 , 32 , 13 , 17 , 12 ] or generating code [ 4 , 20 ] , evaluations also evolved to measure these abilities. A parallel line of work has continued to evaluate LLM abilities on natural language tasks, with a focus on their ability to be creative [ 11 , 38 , 42 ] . However, many evaluations have highlighted the same gap: LLM-outputted text lacks diversity, and on open-ended tasks, tends to converge to similar clusters, even across vastly different families of models [ 19 ] . These evaluations have focused on LLM-generated English outputs without studying the effect of language on output diversity. sections.heading: 2.2 Development of multilingual LLMs.
sections.text: Some of the first multilingual LLMs included Multilingual BERT [ 27 ] , XLM-R [ 6 ] , and BLOOM [ 37 ] . More recent variants include Aya [ 33 ] , and national efforts to train LLMs primarily in a specific language [ 30 , 10 ] . Even popular models like Qwen [ 40 ] and Deepseek [ 8 ] , trained in China, are trained to perform tasks in both English and Mandarin. Despite these efforts, evaluations on parallel multilingual benchmarks still show that LLMs are generally less performant on non-English tasks [ 39 , 1 ] . This highlights the need for additional work in multilingual LLM development. In this work, we identify another gap in the evaluation of multilingual LLMs: their ability to output diverse text. For this, we use the OpenAssistant2 dataset, introduced as a multilingual large-scale alignment dataset for RLHF, to measure multilingual diversity in LLM outputs [ 23 ] .

sections.heading: 3.1 Dataset
sections.text: For our study, we use the OpenAssistant2 Conversations [ 23 ] , a chat dataset spanning 135,174 messages in 28 different languages crowdsourced from 13,500 global volunteers. Because our analysis involves comparing diversity of human-generated responses to that of LLMs, we filter to prompts where 3 or more human responses are available, which narrows the dataset down to 13 languages where most prompts have 3 or more responses, over which we conduct our evaluation. The languages we evaluate are: English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, German, French, Catalan, Brazilian Portuguese, Italian, Japanese, Basque, Polish, and Vietnamese.

sections.heading: 3.2 Models
sections.text: We evaluate models from five open-weight model families: OLMo 2, Qwen3, Gemma 3, Mistral and Aya Expanse. We choose models of a variety of sizes, ranging from 270M–235B, and architectures, including reasoning models and mixtures-of-experts. We use OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small embedding model to measure embedding distances for our diversity metrics. The full list of models, with checkpoint revisions, precision, decoding settings and chat-template details, is provided in Appendix A . Because the geometry of an embedding space reflects the corpus it was trained on, a diversity metric read off a single embedder risks measuring that corpus rather than the generations. We therefore repeat the entire analysis in two further embedding spaces and under a metric that uses no embedding space at all; Section 4.3 reports the result.

sections.text: We measure the diversity of generated text using cosine similarity. Specifically, we define the following metrics: 1. Intra-model similarity. For a given prompt and model, we compute the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings over multiple samples, averaged over all prompts in our dataset. 2. Inter-model similarity. For a given prompt and pair of distinct models, the expected cosine similarity between one random sample from each model. With 50 samples per model we compute this expectation exactly over all 50 × 50 50\times 50 cross-model pairs and average over prompts. 3. Lexical similarity (embedder-free). This estimator has the same form as the cosine metrics above and involves no learned representation; it plays the role Self-BLEU [ 43 ] plays for English-only diversity benchmarks.

sections.heading: Generation.
sections.text: To evaluate the universality of the artificial hivemind effect across different linguistic distributions, we execute a large-scale multilingual generation sweep. Utilizing our filtered prompt set of 390 open-ended prompts across 13 languages from the OpenAssistant2 (OASST2) dataset, we generate output samples with the 23 selected open-weight models. For each individual prompt and model combination, we generate 50 independent response samples. To ensure consistency and align with prior work [ 19 ] , generations are produced using a temperature of 1.0, a top_p threshold of 0.9, a maximum token limit of 2048, and a fixed random seed of 42. We do not vary the decoding configuration, because Jiang et al. [ 19 ] report that even diversity-oriented decoding (min- p p sampling at temperature 2.0 2.0 ) leaves 81% of same-model response pairs above 0.7 0.7 cosine similarity, so decoding can change the size of the effect but is unlikely to remove it. This setup results in a total of 448,500 target generations. Each generated text response is embedded using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model, and the resulting vectors are L 2 L^{2} -normalized prior to metric computation.

sections.heading: Statistical tests.
sections.text: To evaluate statistical significance across the general pool, model families, individual models, and languages, we compare LLM intra- and inter-model similarity against the human baseline with the prompt as the statistical unit. Each (language, prompt) cell contributes one LLM value (the mean pairwise cosine over a model’s 50 samples, averaged over models where models are pooled) and one human value (over the ∼ 3 {\sim}3 human answers), so the non-independent pairwise similarities within a prompt collapse into one observation, and the 50-versus-3 asymmetry affects each prompt’s variance rather than its expectation. The F-tests we report are two-group one-way ANOVAs on these values (390 versus 390 for pooled and per-model tests, 30 versus 30 per language and per (model, language) cell). Because the two sides are paired by prompt and 299 cells are tested, Appendix D repeats every comparison as a paired prompt-level analysis with Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg correction [ 16 , 2 ] . Every conclusion in this section holds under it, and all figure stars and whiskers are drawn from it.

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: Our experiments reveal that the artificial hivemind phenomenon is pervasive across languages, rejecting the hypothesis that mode collapse is solely a localized artifact of English-centric pre-training distributions or reinforcement learning alignment.

sections.heading: Intra-model Clustering.
sections.text: As demonstrated in Figure 6 , language models systematically generate text that clusters tighter than human responses across every evaluated language. We compare one LLM with many humans on purpose. Most people hear from many different humans but consult the same LLM, so a single model that is less diverse than a group of humans can homogenize the thinking of everyone who relies on it. The mean LLM intra-model cosine similarity reaches 0.857 0.857 , compared to the more diverse human baseline score of 0.657 0.657 for the identical prompt set. The F-test confirms that the diversity gap is statistically significant with a value of p < 10 − 88 p<10^{-88} , and the paired prompt-level analysis of Appendix D confirms it for all 23 models, all 13 languages and 271 of the 299 (model, language) cells after Holm correction (Table 4 ). This sets one model, resampled, against ∼ 3 {\sim}3 different human authors, since humans cannot be resampled (Section 6 ). The like-for-like comparison, different models against different humans, follows below and points the same way. The same-model similarity of 0.857 0.857 also exceeds the different-model similarity of 0.750 0.750 , so resampling one model recovers less variety than switching models (Appendix D ). To visually interpret the high-dimensional embedding spaces, we include Per-Language Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projections in Figure 1 , where LLM generations collapse into high-density modes while the human answers are spread thinly over the same region of the embedding space. The within-prompt gap that the tests measure is not visible in a pooled projection. Appendix B shows the same projection for all 13 languages. sections.heading: Inter-model Clustering.
sections.text: To address whether shifting across distinct model choices injects meaningful structural variation into open-ended generations, we analyze cross-model behaviors via the inter-model similarity metric ( L ​ L ​ M ↔ L ​ L ​ M LLM\leftrightarrow LLM ). As shown in Figure 2 , pairs of independent LLMs systematically agree more with each other than pairs of humans responding to the same prompt, across 12 out of the 13 evaluated languages (pooled gap + 0.093 +0.093 , with every family pair and 12 of 13 languages significant after Holm correction, Table 4 ). The exception to this trend occurs in Basque ( eu ), which is the only language in our data where human responses display tighter semantic clustering than that of the LLMs, and that reversal is itself significant. In contrast, for Japanese ( ja ) the model-to-human cosine similarity gap reaches its largest difference of + 0.33 +0.33 , observed for Gemma-3 27B. The respondent–respondent similarity matrix (Figure 9 ) shows the same pattern: most pairs of models are more similar to each other than the human–human baseline of 65.7 65.7 . sections.heading: 4.2 Model- and Family-specific Analysis
sections.text: To investigate the hivemind effect in more detail, we evaluate model specific diversity (Figure 3 ), cross-family interaction (Figure 8 , Appendix C ) and respondent-to-respondent similarity (Figure 4 ). A respondent is one of the 23 LLMs or the pooled human annotators (24 in total); each cell is the mean similarity between two respondents’ answers to the same prompt. The LLM diagonal resamples a single model at T = 1.0 T=1.0 , while the human diagonal compares the ∼ 3 {\sim}3 different annotators per prompt, since humans cannot be resampled. The model-by-language matrix (Figure 3 ) exposes a possible tradeoff between downstream optimization and generative diversity. The OLMo-2 and Mistral families consistently demonstrate high text diversity. We speculate that these models are less heavily steered by hyper-alignment pipelines, resulting in the preservation of more diverse generations. In contrast, the Aya Expanse family [ 7 ] is explicitly instruction-tuned for multilingual tasks, yet it provides less diverse responses across most languages. Similarly, despite heavy pre-training and alignment in Mandarin, Qwen models [ 40 ] output responses with low diversity in Chinese ( zh ). This suggests the possibility that there is a trade-off between model performance and diversity. Low-parameter footprints like Gemma-3 270M and Gemma-3 1B display high diversity in Figure 3 for languages like Japanese ( ja ) and Basque ( eu ). However, qualitative log inspection reveals this is a statistical artifact of generation failure. In non-English environments, the smaller models experience linguistic and syntactic breakdown, resulting in incoherent character strings artificially lowering the mean pairwise cosine similarity. The inter-model homogenization is visible in Figures 4 and 8 . The family-pair heatmap (Figure 8 ) displays higher than human homogeneity across almost all languages and families. This behavior is further illustrated by the respondent–respondent matrix (Figure 4 ), which reveals higher mutual similarity between model families than that of human responses, especially for Qwen3 and Gemma-3. Of the 253 253 distinct LLM–LLM model pairs, 245 245 score above the human–human baseline of 65.7 65.7 , as do all 10 10 family-level pairings (minimum 71.7 71.7 ), indicating lower diversity. The eight exceptions all involve Gemma-3 270M or Qwen3 0.6B, the models whose non-English output degrades into incoherence, so they reflect generation failure rather than genuine diversity.

sections.heading: 5 What Predicts the Per-Language Gap?
sections.text: The hivemind effect holds everywhere, but not equally: in the primary embedding space the mean gap ranges from 0.076 0.076 in Basque to 0.270 0.270 in Russian. Only the low end of that range is stable. Basque has the smallest gap under all five metrics, while the ordering of the other twelve languages agrees well between embedders (Spearman ρ = 0.76 \rho=0.76 – 0.85 0.85 ) and not at all with the embedder-free ranking ( ρ = 0.38 \rho=0.38 , p = 0.20 p=0.20 ). We therefore ask which properties of a language, or of a model’s command of it, account for the spread.

sections.heading: Predictors.
sections.text: We test the four properties suggested by the structure of the problem, two varying per (model, language) and two per language. Tokenization fertility is the number of subword tokens a model’s tokenizer spends on FLORES-200 devtest [ 31 ] , relative to the same tokenizer’s English count. Parallel text keeps the measure a property of the tokenizer rather than of the model’s output distribution. Model competence is the chrF++ [ 28 ] of the model’s zero-shot translation of the 1,012 FLORES+ devtest sentences from English into the language, a held-out task that shares no prompts or outputs with the generations we score. It is undefined for English, which this section therefore omits. The GlotLID [ 22 ] target-language match rate over a cell’s 1500 generations is used only as an outcome-quality filter (specification C) and as a fifth predictor in a comparison fit (specification F). Resource level is log 10 \log_{10} of the language’s Wikipedia article count. Morphological complexity is the type-token ratio of the FLORES parallel text; it is undefined for zh and ja , which lack whitespace word boundaries.

sections.heading: Method.
sections.text: We regress the gap on all four predictors, z z -scored, with crossed random intercepts for model and for language. Crossing matters: resource level and morphology take only 13 distinct values, so a model-only random effect would treat 13 languages as hundreds of independent observations. Two models lack a benchmark score, 1 1 1 Qwen3 235B and Qwen3 30B could not be run on the benchmark hardware, so this section uses the remaining 21 models and, with English as the translation source, 12 languages. All other sections use all 23 models and 13 languages. and one predictor is incomplete. Morphology is undefined for zh and ja , so the full specification (A) fits 21 × 10 = 210 21\times 10=210 cells; dropping morphology (B) recovers zh and ja and uses all 252 252 , and restricting B to cells with a GlotLID match rate of at least 0.80 0.80 (C) leaves 230 230 . Specification F adds the match rate to B as a fifth predictor. No cell is excluded for any other reason.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Fitting the model in all three embedding spaces separates one robust predictor from three that are not (Figure 5 b, Table 6 ). Competence predicts the gap in every space ( β = + 0.036 \beta=+0.036 / + 0.038 +0.038 / + 0.039 +0.039 in specification A, p < 0.001 p<0.001 in every space for specifications A to C). Resource level ( p ≥ 0.13 p\geq 0.13 ), tokenization fertility ( p ≥ 0.10 p\geq 0.10 ) and morphological complexity ( p ≥ 0.12 p\geq 0.12 ) do not predict it in any space. Resource level reaches p < 0.05 p<0.05 only when competence is standardised within each language (specification H, Appendix E ), which hands the between-language part of competence to the resource term, so we do not treat it as robust either way. Homogenization thus tracks how well a model handles a language far more than the language’s typology. Basque, the highest-fertility ( 1.77 × 1.77\times English) and lowest-resource language in our set, and one of the three that models translate into worst, has the smallest gap under every metric we computed. Four checks support this reading: dropping the 22 cells with a GlotLID match rate below 0.80 0.80 (specification C) leaves the coefficient intact in all three spaces ( β = + 0.044 \beta=+0.044 / + 0.044 +0.044 / + 0.043 +0.043 ), so degenerate generation is not what carries it; standardising competence within each language (specification H) leaves it intact as well, so differences in chrF++ between scripts do not carry it; resource level predicts LLM intra-similarity ( ρ = 0.52 \rho=0.52 ) but not human ( ρ = 0.02 \rho=0.02 ), placing the effect on the model side; and fertility predicts raw LLM intra-similarity but largely cancels in the gap, shifting the human side in the same direction. Adding the GlotLID match rate to B as a fifth predictor (F) leaves competence significant in every space ( β = + 0.023 \beta=+0.023 / + 0.029 +0.029 / + 0.029 +0.029 , p ≤ 0.003 p\leq 0.003 ) while the match rate is itself significant ( β = + 0.024 \beta=+0.024 / + 0.018 +0.018 / + 0.018 +0.018 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), so on-language output is associated with homogenization over and above competence. This quantifies the performance–diversity tradeoff suggested in Section 4 as an association: in our data, the better a model’s command of a language, the less diverse what it writes in it. Because the design is observational, we do not claim that improving competence causes the loss of diversity (Section 6 ). sections.heading: Language sample.
sections.text: Our original design called for the 10–20 largest languages by native-speaker count [ 9 ] . To our knowledge, OpenAssistant2 is the only multilingual open-ended corpus with three or more human responses per prompt, and it fixes the 13 languages we study. Together they account for roughly 2.7 2.7 billion native speakers, against roughly 3.9 3.9 billion for the twenty largest, but four languages (Mandarin, Spanish, English, Portuguese) carry that figure: ten of the thirteen are European, and the set contains no language of South Asia, no Arabic, Turkish, Korean, or Indonesian. Basque is the only genuinely low-resource language, so the conclusion that the gap tracks competence rather than typology rests on a narrow typological base.

sections.heading: Non-parallel prompts.
sections.text: OpenAssistant2 prompts are written natively in each language rather than translated, so per-language comparisons conflate the language with its prompt and topic distribution. Model-level results are unaffected (all models answer identical prompts), but part of the per-language variation may be topical.

sections.heading: Human baseline.
sections.text: Each prompt carries ∼ 3 {\sim}3 human responses by different authors, against 50 resamples of each LLM. Humans cannot be resampled, so the human intra-similarity mixes author variance with response variance. This shifts the level of the baseline rather than the sign of the effect, and the like-for-like inter-model test of Section 4.1 points the same way.

sections.heading: Competence measure and causality.
sections.text: Competence is translation quality from English under a surface metric, so English itself is not covered, chrF++ levels are not comparable across scripts (hence the language random effect and specification H), two models lack scores, and the Qwen3 models were run without reasoning. The association in Section 5 is not a causal estimate, since we manipulated neither competence, training data, alignment nor language coverage.

sections.heading: Length control.
sections.text: The 500-character cap was applied to the lexical metric and to BGE-M3 on 10 of the 50 samples per prompt, not to the primary embedder. The intra-model gap is unchanged under the cap, but the cap is a crude form of matching, since it truncates 80% of LLM responses but only 38% of human ones and so sets largely complete human answers against LLM openings. Generations of human-like length would need a new sweep with a length instruction, since in 63% of (model, prompt) cells none of the 50 samples is that short.

sections.heading: Metric stability.
sections.text: The per-language ordering of the gap agrees between embedders but not with the embedder-free metric, and only Basque’s position replicates under all five. Under BGE-M3 the Basque intra-model test loses significance ( p = 0.088 p=0.088 ). The inter-model comparison is reported in the primary embedding space only.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: All generations use one decoding configuration (temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p p 0.9 0.9 , at most 2048 tokens) and the five Qwen3 dense models ran in their default thinking mode (Appendix A ), and the evaluated models are open-weight only. Our conclusions apply to these models, languages, prompts and decoding setting, and proprietary models and other sampling regimes remain untested.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: For the 23 open-weight models, 13 languages and decoding configuration we study, the artificial hivemind phenomenon is in general pervasive and statistically significant across languages, model families and model sizes. The intra-model effect appears in all 13 languages under three different embedding models and under a lexical metric that uses none, so it is not an artifact of the embedding space, and both effects survive paired prompt-level tests corrected for multiple comparisons. Its magnitude is associated with how well a model handles a language, measured on a held-out benchmark, far more than with the language’s typology, so the effect may grow rather than shrink as multilingual coverage improves. We encourage future work to model this performance–diversity tradeoff for multilingual tasks further, and to treat output diversity as an explicit objective that better language coverage alone does not provide.

sections.heading: Appendix A Models and Compute
sections.text: In Table 2 , we include a list of all the model families and models we experiment with, together with the Hugging Face checkpoint and revision of each, the precision it was served at and the GPUs it ran on. Every checkpoint is the instruction-tuned release and was served at the precision declared in its config. Qwen3 235B is an FP8-quantized release.

sections.heading: Prompts and decoding.
sections.text: The 30 prompts per language are OpenAssistant2 root prompts with at least three reviewed human replies, sampled with a fixed seed. The replies form the human baseline. All generations are produced with vLLM [ 24 ] through its chat interface, which applies each checkpoint’s own chat template, with a single user turn and no system prompt. Generation stops at the template’s end-of-turn token or at the 2048-token limit. The five Qwen3 dense checkpoints (0.6B–32B) default to thinking mode and emit a <think> block, which we keep as part of the response when embedding. For the GlotLID match rate used in Section 5 we strip the block first, and a block left unclosed because the token limit was hit counts as a non-match. Of the 448,500 generations, 79 are empty strings and are dropped before embedding.

sections.heading: Embedding and language identification.
sections.text: text-embedding-3-small was queried through the OpenAI API in May 2026. The API exposes no snapshot identifier for embedding models. BGE-M3 [ 3 ] (revision 5617a9f6 ) and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [ 41 ] (revision 97b0c614 ) were run with sentence-transformers at their native sequence limits, which are longer than any generation. Language identification uses GlotLID v3 [ 22 ] (revision 85cd6716 ). For de , ja and zh we also count the closely related labels Swiss German, Hiragana-only Japanese and Wu/Cantonese as matches.

sections.heading: Appendix D Statistical Procedure and Prompt-Level Tests
sections.text: The F-tests in the main text are two-group one-way ANOVAs on the per-prompt values defined in Section 3.4 , with ( 1 , n a + n b − 2 ) (1,n_{a}+n_{b}-2) degrees of freedom, where n a n_{a} and n b n_{b} are the numbers of prompts on the LLM and the human side. The two counts are equal except for Gemma-3 270M, which returned an empty string for all 50 samples of one German prompt, so that cell and that model’s pooled test have one LLM value fewer. The statistic equals t 2 t^{2} for the pooled-variance two-sample t t -test on the same values. Because the LLM and human values are paired by prompt, all significance markers and error bars in the figures come from the paired analysis described below. Whiskers are standard errors over prompts, and stars are Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank p p -values ( ∗ p < 0.05 {}^{*}p<0.05 , p ∗ ⁣ ∗ < 0.01 {}^{**}p<0.01 , ∗ ∗ ∗ p < 0.001 {}^{***}p<0.001 ). For every comparison in the paper we form one difference per prompt, Δ p = LLM p − Human p \Delta_{p}=\text{LLM}_{p}-\text{Human}_{p} , averaging the LLM side over the models or model pairs in the group first, and test Δ p \Delta_{p} against zero with (i) a 95% percentile bootstrap interval over prompts (10,000 resamples), (ii) the Wilcoxon signed-rank test [ 36 ] , and (iii) a sign-flip permutation test of the mean difference (20,000 Monte Carlo permutations). Within each level the p p -values are adjusted across all groups tested at that level by Holm’s step-down procedure [ 16 ] , which controls the family-wise error rate, and by Benjamini–Hochberg [ 2 ] , which controls the false discovery rate. For the pooled gaps we also resample languages as clusters and then prompts within each selected language (10,000 resamples). sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: The checklist is designed to encourage best practices for responsible machine learning research, addressing issues of reproducibility, transparency, research ethics, and societal impact. Do not remove the checklist: The papers not including the checklist will be desk rejected. The checklist should follow the references and follow the (optional) supplemental material. The checklist does NOT count towards the page limit. Please read the checklist guidelines carefully for information on how to answer these questions. For each question in the checklist: • You should answer [Yes] , [No] , or [N/A] . • [N/A] means either that the question is Not Applicable for that particular paper or the relevant information is Not Available. • Please provide a short (1–2 sentence) justification right after your answer (even for [N/A] ). The checklist answers are an integral part of your paper submission. They are visible to the reviewers, area chairs, senior area chairs, and ethics reviewers. You will also be asked to include it (after eventual revisions) with the final version of your paper, and its final version will be published with the paper. The reviewers of your paper will be asked to use the checklist as one of the factors in their evaluation. While [Yes] is generally preferable to [No] , it is perfectly acceptable to answer [No] provided a proper justification is given (e.g., error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive” or “we were unable to find the license for the dataset we used”). In general, answering [No] or [N/A] is not grounds for rejection. While the questions are phrased in a binary way, we acknowledge that the true answer is often more nuanced, so please just use your best judgment and write a justification to elaborate. All supporting evidence can appear either in the main paper or the supplemental material, provided in appendix. If you answer [Yes] to a question, in the justification please point to the section(s) where related material for the question can be found. IMPORTANT, please: • Delete this instruction block, but keep the section heading “NeurIPS Paper Checklist" , • Keep the checklist subsection headings, questions/answers and guidelines below. • Do not modify the questions and only use the provided macros for your answers . 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Abstract and methods/results go hand-in-hand. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 6 is a dedicated Limitations section. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper contains no theoretical results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 3 gives the dataset, models, metrics and decoding settings; Appendix A lists every checkpoint with its Hugging Face revision, precision, hardware, chat-template handling and truncation statistics, together with the embedding and language-identification model versions; Appendix D defines every statistical test. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Code, the prompt-selection procedure and all derived metrics are released at the URL given in Appendix A. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All details are included in the methods section. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The F-tests in the main text are defined in the Methods, with the prompt as the statistical unit. Every star and whisker in the figures comes from the paired prompt-level analysis of Appendix D , where whiskers are standard errors over prompts and stars are Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank p p -values. Table 4 adds bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests and Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix A (Compute paragraph and Table 2) gives GPU types, per-model GPU counts and the total GPU-hours. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have read and meet the NeurIPS code of ethics. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We discuss this in the conclusion. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Answer: [N/A] Justification: We do not release any new data or models. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Answer: [Yes] Justification: The dataset we use is covered under an Apache 2.0 license, and we properly credit and cite their work. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Xaver Raphael Davey Affiliation: KTH Royal Institute of Technology Email: xrdavey@kth.se Shubhra Mishra Affiliation: KTH Royal Institute of Technology Email: shubhram@kth.se Anton Adelöw Affiliation: KTH Royal Institute of Technology Email: aadelow@kth.se Siyao Liu Affiliation: KTH Royal Institute of Technology Email: siyaol@kth.se Abstract Text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) often remains limited in diversity compared to that produced by humans. Recent advances demonstrate the presence of inter- and intra-model collapse in open-ended generation of English text, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of LLM, and more importantly, human thought. However, our understanding of whether this homogenization extends to languages beyond English is limited. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Specifically, we aim to understand whether multilingual LLM-generated text is also homogeneous, and whether this homogeneity matches what we observe in humans. Across 23 open-weight models and 13 languages, we find that the artificial hivemind effect is pervasive but uneven in its extent. The intra-model effect holds in three different embedding spaces and under a lexical metric that uses no embedding model, so it is not an artifact of how diversity is measured. The size of the homogenization gap is associated with a model’s competence in a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, robustly across embedding spaces. Thus, we demonstrate a performance–diversity tradeoff in multilingual LLMs. 1 Introduction In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have become central in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). As their adoption increases, closer examination of the nature of the generated text is warranted. Specifically, empirical evaluations have revealed an artificial hivemind-like effect in open-ended generation [ 19 ] , defined by high levels of inter- and intra-model homogeneity, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of text on the internet. However, the causes of the observed mode collapse remain unclear. Potential explanations for this phenomenon range from inductive biases inherent to the optimization algorithms used, to the diversity and scale of the training distribution. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Figure 1 : Per-language Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projections of response embeddings. For four representative languages (English, Japanese, Basque, and Chinese), blue point clouds represent the spatial distribution of pooled LLM generations, while red × \times markers display the human answers to the same prompts. LLM generations concentrate into dense modes, whereas the human answers are spread thinly over the same region. Each panel pools all 30 prompts of its language, so it shows the mode structure of the pooled distribution rather than the within-prompt gap measured in Section 4 . Each of the two plotted components explains 5–10% of the embedding variance in its panel. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We evaluate output diversity for 23 LLMs for 13 different languages. • We show that the artificial hivemind effect is, in general, pervasive across languages. • We show the intra-model effect is robust to how diversity is measured, replicating it in three embedding spaces and under an embedder-free lexical metric, and that both effects survive paired prompt-level tests with multiple-comparison correction. • We show that the homogenization gap tracks how well a model handles a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, far more than properties of the language itself such as tokenization cost or morphology. 2 Related Work Our work broadly relates to (i) language model evaluation, and (ii) the development of multilingual LLMs. 2.1 Language Model Evaluation As language model architectures and capabilities have evolved, so have the evaluations we use to measure progress. Early evaluations of LLMs focused primarily on natural language processing and understanding tasks like question answering and text-summarization [ 21 , 35 , 34 , 29 ] , often relying on metrics like accuracy for single-answer tasks, and the BLEU or F1 score [ 26 ] for open-ended tasks. As LLMs became more capable of reasoning-based tasks [ 14 ] like solving math problems [ 5 , 15 , 32 , 13 , 17 , 12 ] or generating code [ 4 , 20 ] , evaluations also evolved to measure these abilities. A parallel line of work has continued to evaluate LLM abilities on natural language tasks, with a focus on their ability to be creative [ 11 , 38 , 42 ] . However, many evaluations have highlighted the same gap: LLM-outputted text lacks diversity, and on open-ended tasks, tends to converge to similar clusters, even across vastly different families of models [ 19 ] . These evaluations have focused on LLM-generated English outputs without studying the effect of language on output diversity. Whiskers are standard errors over prompts; stars mark Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on the per-prompt differences (Appendix D ): ∗ p < 0.05 {}^{*}p<0.05 , p ∗ ⁣ ∗ < 0.01 {}^{**}p<0.01 , ∗ ∗ ∗ p < 0.001 {}^{***}p<0.001 . 2.2 Development of multilingual LLMs. Some of the first multilingual LLMs included Multilingual BERT [ 27 ] , XLM-R [ 6 ] , and BLOOM [ 37 ] . More recent variants include Aya [ 33 ] , and national efforts to train LLMs primarily in a specific language [ 30 , 10 ] . Even popular models like Qwen [ 40 ] and Deepseek [ 8 ] , trained in China, are trained to perform tasks in both English and Mandarin. Despite these efforts, evaluations on parallel multilingual benchmarks still show that LLMs are generally less performant on non-English tasks [ 39 , 1 ] . This highlights the need for additional work in multilingual LLM development. In this work, we identify another gap in the evaluation of multilingual LLMs: their ability to output diverse text. For this, we use the OpenAssistant2 dataset, introduced as a multilingual large-scale alignment dataset for RLHF, to measure multilingual diversity in LLM outputs [ 23 ] . 3 Methods 3.1 Dataset For our study, we use the OpenAssistant2 Conversations [ 23 ] , a chat dataset spanning 135,174 messages in 28 different languages crowdsourced from 13,500 global volunteers. Because our analysis involves comparing diversity of human-generated responses to that of LLMs, we filter to prompts where 3 or more human responses are available, which narrows the dataset down to 13 languages where most prompts have 3 or more responses, over which we conduct our evaluation. The languages we evaluate are: English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, German, French, Catalan, Brazilian Portuguese, Italian, Japanese, Basque, Polish, and Vietnamese. 3.2 Models We evaluate models from five open-weight model families: OLMo 2, Qwen3, Gemma 3, Mistral and Aya Expanse. We choose models of a variety of sizes, ranging from 270M–235B, and architectures, including reasoning models and mixtures-of-experts. We use OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small embedding model to measure embedding distances for our diversity metrics. The full list of models, with checkpoint revisions, precision, decoding settings and chat-template details, is provided in Appendix A . Because the geometry of an embedding space reflects the corpus it was trained on, a diversity metric read off a single embedder risks measuring that corpus rather than the generations. We therefore repeat the entire analysis in two further embedding spaces and under a metric that uses no embedding space at all; Section 4.3 reports the result. 3.3 Metrics We measure the diversity of generated text using cosine similarity. We define mean pairwise cosine similarity over embeddings { 𝐳 i } i = 1 n \{\mathbf{z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} as 1 ( n 2 ) ​ ∑ i < j cos ⁡ ( 𝐳 i , 𝐳 j ) = 2 n ⁡ ( n − 1 ) ​ ∑ i < j 𝐳 i ⊤ ​ 𝐳 j ‖ 𝐳 i ‖ 2 ​ ‖ 𝐳 j ‖ 2 . \frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\cos(\mathbf{z}_{i},\mathbf{z}_{j})=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}\frac{\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}\|_{2}}. Specifically, we define the following metrics: 1. Intra-model similarity. For a given prompt and model, we compute the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings over multiple samples, averaged over all prompts in our dataset. 2. Inter-model similarity. For a given prompt and pair of distinct models, the expected cosine similarity between one random sample from each model. With 50 samples per model we compute this expectation exactly over all 50 × 50 50\times 50 cross-model pairs and average over prompts. 3. Lexical similarity (embedder-free). For a given prompt and model we compute the mean pairwise Jaccard similarity [ 18 ] of character 4-gram sets, 2 n ⁡ ( n − 1 ) ​ ∑ i < j | G i ∩ G j | / | G i ∪ G j | \frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}|G_{i}\cap G_{j}|/|G_{i}\cup G_{j}| , where G i G_{i} is the set of character 4-grams of sample i i . We use character rather than word n n -grams because zh and ja have no whitespace word boundaries, and a pairwise rather than a pooled statistic (such as distinct- n n [ 25 ] ) because a cell holds 50 LLM samples but only ∼ 3 {\sim}3 human responses: pooled n n -gram ratios shrink as the pool grows, so a pooled metric would report a large effect from sample count alone. This estimator has the same form as the cosine metrics above and involves no learned representation; it plays the role Self-BLEU [ 43 ] plays for English-only diversity benchmarks. 3.4 Experiments Generation. To evaluate the universality of the artificial hivemind effect across different linguistic distributions, we execute a large-scale multilingual generation sweep. Utilizing our filtered prompt set of 390 open-ended prompts across 13 languages from the OpenAssistant2 (OASST2) dataset, we generate output samples with the 23 selected open-weight models. For each individual prompt and model combination, we generate 50 independent response samples. To ensure consistency and align with prior work [ 19 ] , generations are produced using a temperature of 1.0, a top_p threshold of 0.9, a maximum token limit of 2048, and a fixed random seed of 42. We do not vary the decoding configuration, because Jiang et al. [ 19 ] report that even diversity-oriented decoding (min- p p sampling at temperature 2.0 2.0 ) leaves 81% of same-model response pairs above 0.7 0.7 cosine similarity, so decoding can change the size of the effect but is unlikely to remove it. This setup results in a total of 448,500 target generations. Each generated text response is embedded using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model, and the resulting vectors are L 2 L^{2} -normalized prior to metric computation. Statistical tests. To evaluate statistical significance across the general pool, model families, individual models, and languages, we compare LLM intra- and inter-model similarity against the human baseline with the prompt as the statistical unit. Each (language, prompt) cell contributes one LLM value (the mean pairwise cosine over a model’s 50 samples, averaged over models where models are pooled) and one human value (over the ∼ 3 {\sim}3 human answers), so the non-independent pairwise similarities within a prompt collapse into one observation, and the 50-versus-3 asymmetry affects each prompt’s variance rather than its expectation. The F-tests we report are two-group one-way ANOVAs on these values (390 versus 390 for pooled and per-model tests, 30 versus 30 per language and per (model, language) cell). Because the two sides are paired by prompt and 299 cells are tested, Appendix D repeats every comparison as a paired prompt-level analysis with Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg correction [ 16 , 2 ] . Every conclusion in this section holds under it, and all figure stars and whiskers are drawn from it. 4 Results Our experiments reveal that the artificial hivemind phenomenon is pervasive across languages, rejecting the hypothesis that mode collapse is solely a localized artifact of English-centric pre-training distributions or reinforcement learning alignment. 4.1 Intra- and Inter-Model Clustering Intra-model Clustering. As demonstrated in Figure 6 , language models systematically generate text that clusters tighter than human responses across every evaluated language. We compare one LLM with many humans on purpose. Most people hear from many different humans but consult the same LLM, so a single model that is less diverse than a group of humans can homogenize the thinking of everyone who relies on it. The mean LLM intra-model cosine similarity reaches 0.857 0.857 , compared to the more diverse human baseline score of 0.657 0.657 for the identical prompt set. The F-test confirms that the diversity gap is statistically significant with a value of p < 10 − 88 p<10^{-88} , and the paired prompt-level analysis of Appendix D confirms it for all 23 models, all 13 languages and 271 of the 299 (model, language) cells after Holm correction (Table 4 ). This sets one model, resampled, against ∼ 3 {\sim}3 different human authors, since humans cannot be resampled (Section 6 ). The like-for-like comparison, different models against different humans, follows below and points the same way. The same-model similarity of 0.857 0.857 also exceeds the different-model similarity of 0.750 0.750 , so resampling one model recovers less variety than switching models (Appendix D ). To visually interpret the high-dimensional embedding spaces, we include Per-Language Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projections in Figure 1 , where LLM generations collapse into high-density modes while the human answers are spread thinly over the same region of the embedding space. The within-prompt gap that the tests measure is not visible in a pooled projection. Appendix B shows the same projection for all 13 languages. Figure 3 : Homogenization gap for each language × \times model pair. Red tiles indicate high levels of homogenization compared to humans, while blue tiles indicate higher generative diversity. Stars as in Figure 2 , corrected across the 299 cells. Inter-model Clustering. To address whether shifting across distinct model choices injects meaningful structural variation into open-ended generations, we analyze cross-model behaviors via the inter-model similarity metric ( L ​ L ​ M ↔ L ​ L ​ M LLM\leftrightarrow LLM ). As shown in Figure 2 , pairs of independent LLMs systematically agree more with each other than pairs of humans responding to the same prompt, across 12 out of the 13 evaluated languages (pooled gap + 0.093 +0.093 , with every family pair and 12 of 13 languages significant after Holm correction, Table 4 ). The exception to this trend occurs in Basque ( eu ), which is the only language in our data where human responses display tighter semantic clustering than that of the LLMs, and that reversal is itself significant. In contrast, for Japanese ( ja ) the model-to-human cosine similarity gap reaches its largest difference of + 0.33 +0.33 , observed for Gemma-3 27B. The respondent–respondent similarity matrix (Figure 9 ) shows the same pattern: most pairs of models are more similar to each other than the human–human baseline of 65.7 65.7 . Figure 4 : Respondent–respondent similarity, aggregated by model family. A respondent is any source of an answer to a prompt: one of the 23 LLMs, or the pooled human annotators. Each cell is the mean pairwise cosine similarity between answers from two different respondents to the same prompt, averaged over all prompts and languages ( × 100 \times 100 ). 4.2 Model- and Family-specific Analysis To investigate the hivemind effect in more detail, we evaluate model specific diversity (Figure 3 ), cross-family interaction (Figure 8 , Appendix C ) and respondent-to-respondent similarity (Figure 4 ). A respondent is one of the 23 LLMs or the pooled human annotators (24 in total); each cell is the mean similarity between two respondents’ answers to the same prompt. The LLM diagonal resamples a single model at T = 1.0 T=1.0 , while the human diagonal compares the ∼ 3 {\sim}3 different annotators per prompt, since humans cannot be resampled. The model-by-language matrix (Figure 3 ) exposes a possible tradeoff between downstream optimization and generative diversity. The OLMo-2 and Mistral families consistently demonstrate high text diversity. We speculate that these models are less heavily steered by hyper-alignment pipelines, resulting in the preservation of more diverse generations. In contrast, the Aya Expanse family [ 7 ] is explicitly instruction-tuned for multilingual tasks, yet it provides less diverse responses across most languages. Similarly, despite heavy pre-training and alignment in Mandarin, Qwen models [ 40 ] output responses with low diversity in Chinese ( zh ). This suggests the possibility that there is a trade-off between model performance and diversity. Low-parameter footprints like Gemma-3 270M and Gemma-3 1B display high diversity in Figure 3 for languages like Japanese ( ja ) and Basque ( eu ). However, qualitative log inspection reveals this is a statistical artifact of generation failure. In non-English environments, the smaller models experience linguistic and syntactic breakdown, resulting in incoherent character strings artificially lowering the mean pairwise cosine similarity. The inter-model homogenization is visible in Figures 4 and 8 . The family-pair heatmap (Figure 8 ) displays higher than human homogeneity across almost all languages and families. This behavior is further illustrated by the respondent–respondent matrix (Figure 4 ), which reveals higher mutual similarity between model families than that of human responses, especially for Qwen3 and Gemma-3. Of the 253 253 distinct LLM–LLM model pairs, 245 245 score above the human–human baseline of 65.7 65.7 , as do all 10 10 family-level pairings (minimum 71.7 71.7 ), indicating lower diversity. The eight exceptions all involve Gemma-3 270M or Qwen3 0.6B, the models whose non-English output degrades into incoherence, so they reflect generation failure rather than genuine diversity. 4.3 Robustness to the Choice of Similarity Metric All results above are computed in one embedding space, and the geometry of that space reflects the corpus it was trained on. An English-heavy training corpus could in principle place non-English generations closer together for reasons unrelated to their diversity. We therefore re-embed all 448,500 generations in two further spaces and recompute the intra-model metric there and under a similarity measure that uses no embedding space at all (Table 1 ). The inter-model comparison of Figure 2 is reported in the primary space only. Table 1 : The homogenization gap under three embedding spaces and an embedder-free lexical metric. Our original design called for the 10–20 largest languages by native-speaker count [ 9 ] . To our knowledge, OpenAssistant2 is the only multilingual open-ended corpus with three or more human responses per prompt, and it fixes the 13 languages we study. Together they account for roughly 2.7 2.7 billion native speakers, against roughly 3.9 3.9 billion for the twenty largest, but four languages (Mandarin, Spanish, English, Portuguese) carry that figure: ten of the thirteen are European, and the set contains no language of South Asia, no Arabic, Turkish, Korean, or Indonesian. Basque is the only genuinely low-resource language, so the conclusion that the gap tracks competence rather than typology rests on a narrow typological base. Non-parallel prompts. OpenAssistant2 prompts are written natively in each language rather than translated, so per-language comparisons conflate the language with its prompt and topic distribution. Model-level results are unaffected (all models answer identical prompts), but part of the per-language variation may be topical. Human baseline. Each prompt carries ∼ 3 {\sim}3 human responses by different authors, against 50 resamples of each LLM. Humans cannot be resampled, so the human intra-similarity mixes author variance with response variance. This shifts the level of the baseline rather than the sign of the effect, and the like-for-like inter-model test of Section 4.1 points the same way. Competence measure and causality. Competence is translation quality from English under a surface metric, so English itself is not covered, chrF++ levels are not comparable across scripts (hence the language random effect and specification H), two models lack scores, and the Qwen3 models were run without reasoning. The association in Section 5 is not a causal estimate, since we manipulated neither competence, training data, alignment nor language coverage. Length control. The 500-character cap was applied to the lexical metric and to BGE-M3 on 10 of the 50 samples per prompt, not to the primary embedder. The intra-model gap is unchanged under the cap, but the cap is a crude form of matching, since it truncates 80% of LLM responses but only 38% of human ones and so sets largely complete human answers against LLM openings. Generations of human-like length would need a new sweep with a length instruction, since in 63% of (model, prompt) cells none of the 50 samples is that short. Metric stability. The per-language ordering of the gap agrees between embedders but not with the embedder-free metric, and only Basque’s position replicates under all five. Under BGE-M3 the Basque intra-model test loses significance ( p = 0.088 p=0.088 ). The inter-model comparison is reported in the primary embedding space only. Scope. All generations use one decoding configuration (temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p p 0.9 0.9 , at most 2048 tokens) and the five Qwen3 dense models ran in their default thinking mode (Appendix A ), and the evaluated models are open-weight only. Our conclusions apply to these models, languages, prompts and decoding setting, and proprietary models and other sampling regimes remain untested. 7 Conclusion For the 23 open-weight models, 13 languages and decoding configuration we study, the artificial hivemind phenomenon is in general pervasive and statistically significant across languages, model families and model sizes. The intra-model effect appears in all 13 languages under three different embedding models and under a lexical metric that uses none, so it is not an artifact of the embedding space, and both effects survive paired prompt-level tests corrected for multiple comparisons. Its magnitude is associated with how well a model handles a language, measured on a held-out benchmark, far more than with the language’s typology, so the effect may grow rather than shrink as multilingual coverage improves. We encourage future work to model this performance–diversity tradeoff for multilingual tasks further, and to treat output diversity as an explicit objective that better language coverage alone does not provide. Appendix A Models and Compute In Table 2 , we include a list of all the model families and models we experiment with, together with the Hugging Face checkpoint and revision of each, the precision it was served at and the GPUs it ran on. Every checkpoint is the instruction-tuned release and was served at the precision declared in its config. Qwen3 235B is an FP8-quantized release. Prompts and decoding. The 30 prompts per language are OpenAssistant2 root prompts with at least three reviewed human replies, sampled with a fixed seed. The replies form the human baseline. All generations are produced with vLLM [ 24 ] through its chat interface, which applies each checkpoint’s own chat template, with a single user turn and no system prompt. Generation stops at the template’s end-of-turn token or at the 2048-token limit. The five Qwen3 dense checkpoints (0.6B–32B) default to thinking mode and emit a <think> block, which we keep as part of the response when embedding. For the GlotLID match rate used in Section 5 we strip the block first, and a block left unclosed because the token limit was hit counts as a non-match. Of the 448,500 generations, 79 are empty strings and are dropped before embedding. Embedding and language identification. text-embedding-3-small was queried through the OpenAI API in May 2026. The API exposes no snapshot identifier for embedding models. BGE-M3 [ 3 ] (revision 5617a9f6 ) and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [ 41 ] (revision 97b0c614 ) were run with sentence-transformers at their native sequence limits, which are longer than any generation. Language identification uses GlotLID v3 [ 22 ] (revision 85cd6716 ). For de , ja and zh we also count the closely related labels Swiss German, Hiragana-only Japanese and Wu/Cantonese as matches. Compute. All experiments are inference-only. Generations were produced with vLLM on a SLURM cluster using NVIDIA A40 (48 GB) and A100 (80 GB) GPUs; the full sweep fit within 130 GPU-hours. Embedding used the OpenAI API plus a few hours on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB), and all downstream analysis runs on CPU. The statistic equals t 2 t^{2} for the pooled-variance two-sample t t -test on the same values. Because the LLM and human values are paired by prompt, all significance markers and error bars in the figures come from the paired analysis described below.
